V. **5**. *{The son of Nahor}* He was the immediate son of Bethuel his father, and Nahor was his grandfather; yet is he named the son rather of Nahor than of Bethuel, because Nahor was a man of more note. See Chap. 31.53. not only in the family of Isaac, as being his father's brother, but in the family of Laban, as appears, Chap. 31.53.

V. **6**. *{Is he well}* Heb. *is there peace to him?* or, *is he in peace?* By which word the Hebrews signify all prosperity: and they call war *Milchamah*, from eating, because it devours all things. Of this expression, see annot. on Chap. 37.14.

*{Lo, it is yet high day}* Heb. *the day is great.* That is, the sun is yet high, and much day to come; and therefore too soon to gather the cattle from their meat; and for those sheep that are already gathered, water them, and bring them back again to their pastures.

V. **8**. *{We cannot until}* It seems the stone that covered the well was so great, that until the shepherds came together, it could not be removed, and that none might be left without aid, they agreed to tarry one for another. So some came sooner, some later, which gave Jacob occasion (having himself been accustomed to the keeping of cattle) to give them his advice out of his good will; and it is not better meant on Jacob's, than taken on the shepherds' part, who do not snap him up as an overbusy stranger, as the Sodomites did Lot, for meddling in matters that belonged not to him, but fairly and gently give an excuse why they cannot follow his advice: which may be an example of meekness, and humanity, and modesty in our intercourse with others, especially strangers.

V. **9**. *{And while he yet spake}* See Gen. 24.15.

*{Rachel}* Not Leah, whose tender eyes could not so well endure the light and open air, ver. 17.

*{with her fathers sheep}* See annot. on Gen. 24.15.

V. **10**. *{Rolled the stone}* With the help of others, or of himself; for being about 77 years of age, the time of full strength in those times, he might haply be able to do that alone, which required the assistance of many hands, especially if the shepherds were young boys, or weak women; and he would strain his strength the more, to be the more noted, and better accepted by Rachel. See the like Exod. 2.17.

V. **11**. *{Kissed Rachel}* Having showed first who he was, and how near of kin, he kissed her, both according to the common fashion among kinsfolks, and out of special affection, as having a mind to take her for a wife: in divers times and countries, the use of kissing has been various: it was sometimes used among men, as ver. 13. of this chapter, and Chap. 31.55. and 45.15. Exod. 4.27. & chap. 18.7. & Luk. 7.45. though most usually betwixt them of a different sex, as a sign of benevolence and love; hence it is applied to express the dear love betwixt Christ and his church, Cant. 1.2. and that the apostle gave order to greet one another with an holy kisse, 2 Cor. 13.12. an holy kiss, not a wanton one, as Prov. 7.13. not an hypocritical kiss, as that of Joab, 2 Sam. 20.9. and of Judas, Mat. 26.49.

*{lifted up his voice and wept}* For joy, after upon mutual report and speech of the state and condition of the several families of Isaac and Laban, and their near kindred; and no doubt also upon the apprehension of God's especial providence in bringing Rachel to the well, (as Rebekah his mother when she was chosen for a wife for his father) his heart melted into affections, that could not be kept in, but burst out into audible and visible expressions, such as might both be heard and seen. See Gen. 45.14, 15, 16.

V. **12**. *{brother}* So ver. 15. That is, near kinsman, for he says in this verse, that he was Rebekah's son, who was Laban's sister, so ver. 15. By this term, brother, was pointed an affection belonging to the nearest degree of kindred that can be; so Lot is called Abraham's brother, being the son of his brother, Gen. 13.8.

V. **13**. *{All these things}* That is, the story of his father's family, and of his journey, the cause why he came from his father's house, and what he had seen by the way.

V. **14**. *{My bone and my flesh}* That is, of my kindred, Gen. 2.23. Judg. 9.2. 2 Sam. 5.1. & 19.13.

*{a month}* Heb. *a month of dayes.* That is, a whole month, not one day short.

V. **18**. *{I will serve thee seven years for Rachel}* It was the custom of many countries to buy wives, whereof there are some instances among the posterity of Jacob, as 1 Sam. 18.25. 2 Sam. 3.14. Hos. 3.2. See also Gen. 34.12. But because Jacob had nothing to give, coming an empty wayfaring man, with a staff in his hand, he offers seven years' service for the younger sister.

V. **19**. *{It is better}* Laban makes no direct answer to Jacob's motion, but gives him good words in the general, without any intent, it seems, to let him so soon be possessed of his choice in particular; Jacob was a plain man, Gen. 25.27. of too honest an heart to suspect deceitful dealing in his uncle; else he was wise enough (as his dealing with his brother Esau shows) to have made a surer bargain for himself.

V. **20**. *{But a few days}* Heb. *one dayes*, Gen. 27.44. If we loved God, our service of him, though it were for many years together, would not be tedious to us; the want of love to him makes men weary to serve him, Mal. 1.13. though but for a few hours, one day in a week, Amos 8.5. the day that should and would (if our affections were rightly tempered) yield us more delight than any of the rest. See Isa. 58.14.

V. **25**. *{Behold it was Leah}* It was Leah before, but then he did behold her, and saw her without her veil; for virgins in modesty were veiled, or brought in the dark to the bride-chamber.

*{beguiled me}* The cause why Jacob was deceived, was, for that in old time the wife was covered with a veil when she was brought to her husband, in sign or token of chastity and shamefastness. See Chap. 24.65. And whereas it is said, that Judah thought Thamar to be an harlot, because she had covered her face, Chap. 38.15. the meaning is, that because her face was covered he knew her not, and because he knew her not, he took her for an harlot; or if harlots did wear veils, they were of another fashion, or worn at other times, and in another manner than brides were wont to do; and though Leah might have been known to Jacob by her speech in the dark, as Jacob's voice was known to Isaac when he was blind, yet her veil might be a cover for her silence, for in that the modesty of women appears, as well as by hiding of their faces; or her speech, being only a low whispering, it could not easily be discerned. In this deceit, it is like that Leah acted her part after her father's, as Jacob his after his mother's direction, and therein she was faulty, though in an inferior degree, for he showed himself a very unjust man, and an unkind uncle; whereby yet Jacob might be remembered of his deceitful dealing with his brother Esau. See Mat. 7.12. though God turned it to good, and might upon this occasion, be disposed to repentance for what was past, and to patience under that condition, which either his necessity, or his uncle's dishonesty put upon him.

V. **26**. *{Not so done in our Country}* Or, *it is not the custome of our Country*. If it had been so, he should have said so much to Jacob seven years sooner, when he offered his service upon condition to marry the younger daughter; this mental reservation of the custom all this while, showed it was not Laban's custom to deal uprightly; besides, if it were the custom, why did he against custom pretend a marriage, and call his neighbors to a marriage feast betwixt Jacob and Rachel? This pretense of custom is often used against truth and right; as in the prohibition of marriage to the clergy, and the communion cup to the laity, and other particulars of the Romish religion; which indeed in respect of the antiquity of truth, are but innovations, though obtruded in the name of ancient customs.

V. **27**. *{Fulfil her week}* The word *Shebang* in Hebrew, is sometimes taken for *seven years*, (so the Geneva translation has it) sometimes for *seven days or a week*, so here; the meaning is, that, forasmuch as the manner was to celebrate a wedding with seven days' feasting, as Judg. 14.12. Jacob should accept of Leah for his wife, and celebrate the nuptials after the wonted manner, and that done, he would presently give him Rachel, for whom he should serve the next *seven years* after, which he did; and that he stayed not for Rachel until a week of years, is evident by order of the story, for Jacob stayed in Mesopotamia with Laban twenty years, chap. 31.38, 41. At the fourteenth year of his servitude was Joseph born, before which time Rachel had been some good while a barren wife, and therefore as out of hope of issue by herself, she gave her maid Bilhah to her husband, who by him had two sons before herself had any, as Gen. 30. shows, whence it must necessarily be concluded, that Jacob was married to Rachel after a week of days, according to the phrase and custom already observed, not after the end of the second *seven years*' service.

V. **28**. *{Fulfilled her week}* That is, he took Leah for his wife, and fulfilled her week of solemn feasting for the wedding, as has been said.

*{Rachel his daughter to wife also}* Two wives at once, if they had not been sisters, had been one too many for one man, as is implied in the first institution of marriage; yet besides them he had both their handmaids to be his wives, Gen. 30. ver. 4, 9. The law against plurality of wives was not yet expressly declared, nor against the marriage of two sisters as afterwards it was, Lev. 18.18. it is doubted therefore, whether at this time either the one or the other were a sin in the holy patriarch; it seems not likely that they having such revelations from God, should be ignorant whether it were a sin or no, or that being so godly, they should live so long in a sin against their knowledge; there was doubtless a disposition of the divine providence in it, if not a dispensation by divine authority for it. For that should not be hastily presumed, since the chief warrant that can be pretended for polygamy, or marriage of many wives at once, is for increase of mankind, and at the first creation in Adam's time, and the renovation of the world in Noah's time, when there was most need of such means of multiplication, God allotted but one woman for one man; and for such like particulars as this of Jacob, though God have his hand in them, ruling and overruling them at his pleasure, and his part be always pure and perfect, yet on man's part there may be corruption and infirmity, as in the matter of the benediction of Jacob, wherein concurred both God and Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob and Esau: God being altogether just and holy in his act, they in theirs were everyone faulty, though in a different degree; yet for the marriage of Jacob (though unlawful, at least doubtful) it may in part be excused, in that his mind was to have had but one, and though he loved that one so affectionately, that seven years' service seemed to him but a few days for her sake, ver. 20. and though he lived with her continually, he modestly and chastely conversed with her all the while: now that Rachel and Leah made offer of their handmaids to his bed, as his grandmother Sarah to his grandfather, and that he accepted of their society, not for pleasure but for propagation to increase mankind, especially to beget children for God's church, such examples must be no patterns for our imitation; yet of polygamy, or having more wives than one, see annot. on Deut. 17.17.

V. **30**. *{Seven years}* After one seven already spent, and so great wrong put upon him, he without murmuring, submits his mind and body to seven years' service more: a rare example of humility and patience.

V. **31**. *{The Lord saw}* God sees not only the actions of men that appear, but their affections that keep out of sight.

*{that Leah was hated, he opened}* That is, less loved; as Matth. 10.37. compared with Luke 14.26. and Joh. 12.25. Rachel had beauty to make her acceptable to Jacob; and to make Leah lovely in his sight, God makes her fruitful, while the other was barren: if Leah had been as fair as Rachel, or Rachel as fruitful as Leah, there would have been too great a prelation of one before the other. Now God, who divides and dispenses his favors as he pleases, qualifies them both in different kinds to be pleasing to their husband, and to moderate the affections of Jacob, that he may neither hate the one, nor dote upon the other: favor and fruitfulness, and every desirable thing, is his free gift, who shows hereby, that oft-times they who are despised of men, are favored of God. See on chap. 8.7.

V. **33**. *{LORD hath heard}* Hereby it appears, that she had recourse to God in her affliction by her complaint; wherein she did not instruct God in her estate, (as if he knew it not without her telling) but sue to him for removal of her affliction, by the obtainment of her husband's affection; and therein the Lord showed that he heard her, by making her amiable as a mother, who was not beloved as a wife.

*{Judah}* In this and the precedent names, she keeps a memorial of God's mercies to her; and as he goes on in grace to her, so does she in gratitude towards him; no barren wife to Jacob her husband, nor barren daughter to God her Father.

## CHAPTER XXX.

Vers. **1**. *{Envied}* The word in the original, is sometimes taken for a lawful emulation in a good cause; sometimes for an unlawful indignation at good; so is the word zeal diversely used in the New Testament; in this place it appears to be set down in a sinful sense, as Rachel's fault to be much offended at her sister's fruitfulness, herself being barren; she should have rejoiced in zeal to God's glory in propagation of the promised seed, in the good of mankind by the multiplication of people, in the increase of God's church, she should have been glad of the blessing of her own flesh and blood, especially in the nearest degree, as Leah was to her, and in the contentment of her husband, (who had no doubt a great desire to be a father, as well as she to be a mother) in that her defect of fruitfulness was supplied by her sister; but self-love makes her sin against them all. Anger is a passion that is sometimes good, else the apostle would not have said, *Be angry and sin not*, Ephes. 4.26. But envy at another's good, Gen. 37.11. Numb. 11.29. Psal. 106.16. is always bad, and so much worse than anger when it is bad, as it is of longer continuance; anger is said to be a short madness, and envy may be said to be a long one. See Prov. 27.4. Gen. 37.11. Wherein we may see the deformity and foulness of envy, the infirmity of human nature, and of the female sex, even in the better sort of women; the disquietness of polygamy, or divers wives at once, even in the most holy, and best ordered family.

*{said unto Jacob, give}* Envy is a sinful and foolish passion, as well as wrath, Job 5.2. It makes Rachel mistake her husband for her God, as her husband did Leah for her, though God were not veiled as Leah was, but she blinded as Jacob was not. Thus does natural corruption break out of one sin into another; she begins with envy at her sister, but proceeds to injury against God, and her injury is no less than idolatry; so though she gave over her father's idols, she became an idolatress again, Jacob's question implies a conviction of her for that sin.

*{else I die}* Not only because she was not to live in her posterity, as her sister Leah in hers, (for the parents may be said to live in that their seed lives in their children) nor that she meant to lay violent hands upon herself, (as some have conceived) but because if she continued childless she had no desire to live, or conceived the grief of her barrenness, would break her heart, and she should die of discontent; for as Eliphaz says, *Envy slayeth the silly one*, Job 5.2. and so it is both a sin, and a punishment of sin. The cause why she was so desirous of children, might be, because fruitfulness was pronounced as a blessing, and to want it, was conceived to be a curse, and so was taken as for a reproach. So ver. 23. and Luke 1.25. 1 Sam. 1.6. Isai. 4.1. That Jacob might delight in her as fruitful, as well as fair, and that her sister might not have that, either as advantage above her, or matter of equality with her; for if she might not be his only beloved, she would be at least, his best beloved bedfellow, which she had cause at least to doubt, for Leah brought him children while she was barren. See on chap. 35.18.

V. **2**. *{Jacobs anger}* A good man may be angry, and it is a good anger when it is set against sin, especially when it shows, that we prefer the honor of God before the favor of our dearest friend, as Jacob here does. See Luk. 14.26.

*{am I in Gods stead}* The godly take it ill that any honor is given to them which is peculiar to God, Act. 14.14, 15. Doubtless the saints and angels above, are not well pleased with the idolatrous services of men below, Rev. 19.10. and 22.9.

*{who hath with-held}* It is only God that makes barren and fruitful, therefore I am not in fault, Gen. 16.2.; 20.18. Psal. 113.9. and 127.3. Hos. 9.14.

V. **3**. *{My maid Bilhah}* Rachel deserved, and had a reproof in the precedent words, which she took with patience, making no reply for her own defense; and seeking to make amends for it, she makes offer of her maid in her stead to her husband's bed, whereby she might have the name of a mother, in the right of her handmaid, for the children that were the handmaid's by nature, were the dame's by adoption; as Gen. 16.2. or by right of participation with her husband, as wherein she had a secondary right, though they were her husband's in the first place, Exod. 21.4. So she made account some part of her barrenness was put away, and some of her husband's good will swayed from her sister (whose envious rival she was) to herself.

*{bear upon my knees}* The meaning is not only that Rachel would receive her children on her lap, as though they were her own; as Gen. 50.23. Isai. 66.12. but that at the birth of them she would do the office of an assistant to the mother, who is many times set upon the knees of another woman while the midwife does her office, and this assistance belonged especially to such as were to be adopting mothers to the children.

V. **4**. *{Handmaid to wife}* Though there be a difference betwixt a wife and a concubine, as has been noted upon Chap. 22.24. and 25.1. yet they agree so much, that the wife is sometimes called a concubine, as Keturah, 1 Chr. 1.32. and a concubine called a wife; as Gen. 16.3. and as Bilhah is here called a wife, so is Zilpah titled, v. 9. and as wives, their children had their portion of inheritance of the land of Canaan with the children of their mistresses, Leah and Rachel; which in other cases was not usual.

V. **6**. *{God hath judged me}* It is like that the emulation betwixt Leah and Rachel, Jacob's wives, as it bred envy on the one side (for ver. 1. Rachel envied Leah for her fruitfulness) so it raised some proud contempt on the other, as in Hagar towards her mistress Sarah, Gen. 16.4. or some reproachful provocation, as in fruitful Peninnah towards barren Hannah, 1 Sam. 1.2, 6. as if God were against them, or had no regard unto them, whom he suffered to be barren; hereupon Rachel making her complaint, and prayer unto God, and making him judge of her cause (as Sarah did of hers, Gen. 16.5.) God blessing her advice and offer of her handmaid with the birth of a child, she takes it to be his judging of the matter on her side, against her emulous sister, who perhaps upbraided her with barrenness, as Peninnah did Hannah; wherein (though God be always just) she was somewhat partial to herself; as ver. 18.

V. **8**. *{With great wrestlings}* Or, *Excellent wrestlings*, in the original, *wrestlings of God*. See the annot. on chap. 23.6. Jonah 3.3. with the places quoted in the margin. She had been very emulous, and striven much with her sister to match her in her fruitfulness; and for that purpose had done what she could to endear herself into the love of Jacob, and had used all the helps she could of diet and physic, and no doubt had with much importunity (like unto her husband's wrestling with God) begged the blessing of the womb for herself, and her handmaid, and so prevailed for another son; but in this boasting, though she accounted herself to be strong in wrestling, she betrayed the weakness of her sex, and the vanity of her mind, for her sister yet had more children than she, and those more her own than Rachel's were.

V. **9**. *{Left bearing}* (Chap. 19.35.) For a time, for she conceived again, and she had children afterwards, ver. 17.

*{Zilpah her handmaid, and gave her to Jacob to wife}* Leah meant in this to match Rachel (for there was striving and wrestling on both sides for the preeminence, both as wives and as mothers; an evil usually incident to polygamy, or multiplication of wives to one husband;) but what Rachel did in a kind of necessity, having no child at all, Leah did without necessity having children already begotten, and born of her own body, as thinking it not honor enough for her to go before her sister in her own immediate fruitfulness, if she did not show herself as kind to her husband in the gift of her handmaid, and matched her sister in that secondary motherhood of the handmaid's issue, wherein she showed herself a sister in evil, being as vain in her desires as Rachel in her boastings.

V. **10**. *{Bear Jacob a son}* It appears Jacob accepted of her gift according to her mind, which shows that Jacob was too indulgent both to his wives and to himself: such human frailties are to be noted, pitied and prayed against, and with all care and caution to be shunned.

V. **11**. *{A troop}* That is, either that at the birth of Gad, there was hope of a plentiful issue increasing to a troop, or that Gad should be a captain of a troop, an eminent man leading others after him.

V. **14**. *{Reuben}* Supposed at this time to be a child about five years old.

*{wheat harvest}* The latter harvest for barley was ripe and reaped before it.

*{Mandrakes}* The word *Dudaim*, in the original (which some translations have retained) in the general signifies *amiable*, as in Cant. 7.13. and is used in this acception, and nowhere else in the whole Scripture; there *Dudaim* is said to give a smell, and it is meant a pleasant smell; thence some translate it *amiable flowers*, the Greek turns it, *apples of Mandragoras*, which is a kind of herb, whose root has the likeness of a man. The fruit of that root called mandrake apples, have been anciently conceived to be of an amorous operation, causing love, conducing to coition and conception; it is said to be of pleasant smell and color by some writers; others say, it is of a rank and unpleasant savor; howsoever it is not like to be mandrake apples, because at this time of the year (which was wheat harvest, and that was about the beginning of May in this country) the mandrake apples are not ripe, but rather that *Dudaim* here rendered mandrakes, was some flowers of the field, (such as pleased little children chiefly with their color, for Reuben that gathered them was about five or six years old) and had withal a delightful smell, Cant. 7.12, 13. so that Rachel was taken with an especial delight in them, and desire of them.

V. **15**. *{Is it a small matter}* Leah not well pleased with Rachel before, takes a small occasion to break out into a passion, the grudge which lay at her heart, now breaks out at her lips, in this question, implying that she makes a small matter of doing to her a great wrong, which she aggravates by adding one wrong unto another.

*{taken my husband}* It seems now Rachel and Leah in respect of childbearing, were both alike; (for though Leah had been fruitful before, she was at that time barren as Rachel, having given over to bear, Chap. 29. ver. 35. and Chap. 30. ver. 9.) and therefore Jacob's affection swayed by the beauty of Rachel, estranged him altogether, or, for the most part, from her bed, thence she challenges her for taking away her husband from her; wherein (but that her self-love made her blind) she might see her sin recompensed to her in its kind; for she had wronged Rachel so before, when it could not but be very offensive unto her.

*{shall lie with thee}* She made ill use of her husband's great affection to her, for here she takes upon her the disposal of his person, and for a trifle hires him out unto her sister.

*{to night}* It seems there was some set rule betwixt Jacob and his wives for their lying with him by turns, so that having a certain right for his society, they might give it up to each other as they could agree.

V. **16**. *{I have hired thee}* That such particulars of seeming small moment are so punctually recorded in the Scripture, the reason may be, to show how observant God is of the family of the faithful, and his providence towards them, which reaches even to the numbering of their hairs, Mat. 10.30.

*{and he lay with her}* The good man, desirous to keep peace betwixt two emulous women, submits to their passions and partialities, and makes good the bargain betwixt them concerning himself, though it were made without his consent.

V. **17**. *{God hearkened to Leah}* This was commendable in both these women, that they invited God by prayer unto their marriage bed, ver. 22.

V. **18**. *{Because I have given}* Though Leah say right in accounting a child to be the gift of God, yet here she misapplies the divine favor, and makes it the reward of her former error, rather than the grant of her precedent prayer; here again she bewrays her infirmity.

V. **22**. *{Hearkened to her}* See annot. on ver. 17.

V. **23**. *{Taken away my reproach}* A reproach among those especially who are fruitful themselves, and therefore show contempt towards the barren, to their disgrace and vexation. See Chap. 16.5. and 1 Sam. 1.5, 6.

V. **26**. *{Give me my wives}* They were already given; or rather dear bought with long and hard service; yet he would not take them away without a mannerly preface of leave from their father before their parting; which condemns the injurious dealing of many, who make no conscience of stealing away daughters, to make them wives without their parents' consent. See annot. on Chap. 21.21.

V. **27**. *{For thy sake}* (Chap. 19.3.) Masters may here learn to make choice of godly servants, in whose hands their estates are like to prosper. Chap. 39.3, 5.

V. **30**. *{Since my coming}* Heb. *At my feet.* That is, since I set my foot into their dwelling, or since I set my foot to labor and go about upon your affairs. See Deut. 11.10.

V. **31**. *{Not give me any thing}* That is, no set rate or price for my service, or (as some think) no recompense out of your precedent or present estate, but out of that which shall accrue unto you from the date of our present agreement.

V. **32**. *{Of such shall be my hire}* That is, when all the speckled, spotted, or particolored, or brown sheep, or lambs, and all the spotted, speckled, or particolored goats are removed, and none left but those that are white, I will have none other wages than those young ones, which coming of white dams, are not white, but particolored or brown; and as there were any brown, he gave them to Laban, and kept only the white, (as Laban's stock to breed upon) lest his particolored increase should be thought to proceed from the different colors of the rams or dams.

V. **33**. *{Righteousness answer}* God shall testify my righteous dealing by rewarding my labors. So that when my stock is increased, it will plainly appear, that the hand of God has been good to me, not mine false or unfaithful to you.

*{in time to come}* Heb. *to morrow*. For that is taken for the time to come, as *yesterday* for the time past, Gen. 31.2. Exod. 4.10. and 5.7. Ruth 2.11. as *today*, for the time present, Psal. 65.7. Heb. 3.7. and 13.8. See on Jos. 22.18.

*{stolen with me}* If he had any of the increase of Laban's sheep or goats, that were not spotted, he would be contented they should be accounted his not by God's gift, but by his own theft.

V. **37**. *{Took rods}* And peeled part, and left part unpeeled, so that they were partly white, and partly green, or of that color they were of before they were peeled: Jacob here uses no deceit, for it was by God's direction, as is probably gathered, Chap. 31.9, 10, 11, 12. and this he did at the ramming time.

*{green poplar}* Not in respect of color but of tenderness and moisture being young, and not hard and dry by growth or age. See Isid. Etymol. l. 12. c. 1. And he took rods of such trees, either because they were more ready at hand, or for some natural quality (though unknown to us) inclining to such an effect as he desired; or God who ordered this device for good success, directed Jacob to this choice.

V. **39**. *{Conceived before the rods}* And particolored according to the rods; this was partly by the strength of imagination, which sometime has great force to conform the conception to the object; so women with child have brought forth children resembling the pictures set before them, sometimes very beautiful, and sometimes very deformed, according to the representation of the pictures in their sight or thought, at the time of their conception: but this was not all, for as it is like that God directed Jacob to this course, so he blessed it to him, that the effect did certainly fall out whensoever the means was used to that purpose, Gen. 31.10, 11, 12. which otherwise had been very uncertain, and more like to fail than to take effect; for such an operation of the fancy or imagination is very rare, especially in the unreasonable creatures; howsoever Jacob must not neglect any means, that God prescribes: and by this we are taught so to order our confidence in God, as not to neglect any human providence, which he either prescribes, or allows.

*{ring straked}* That is, having a streak of contrary colors about their leg round like a ring.

V. **40**. *{Faces of the flocks toward the ring straked}* This was, that by looking upon them their imaginations might work to a resemblance of them, which by concurrence of God's power in favor to Jacob, produced effects, though in that kind rare, yet very regular for the increase of his riches, to a liberal reward of his good service.

V. **41**. *{The stronger cattle}* Which took the ram about September, and brought forth about March; but the feebler took ram in March, and yeaned about September: yet some conceive the quite contrary, and for such cattle as bring forth twice a year (as the sheep in Mesopotamia do, and the like observation is made of the sheep in Italy) the latter birth may be accounted the feebler, for the firstborn has the might and beginning of strength, as Jacob said of Reuben, Gen. 49.3. and the Hebrew word *Hagnatiph*, sounds to that sense, for it signifies both *late bringing forth*, and *feebleness*; and when the feebler engendered, he laid no colored rods before them.

V. **42**. *{So the feebler were Labans}* Laban dealt subtly with Jacob, in putting it to him to set down the condition touching his wages, thinking his modesty would demand less than fully to answer his desert; and to prevent Jacob's subtle dealing with him, he put his particolored cattle to the keeping of his own sons, and committed the rest unto Jacob's custody, yet is Jacob's portion increased, and Laban's diminished.

V. **43**. *{Increased exceedingly}* The means whereby this came to pass, he mentions to his wives, where he says, *God hath taken away the cattel of your father, and given them unto me*, Chap. 31.9. wherein God dealt kindly with him as a son, while his uncle did him not the justice due to a servant; how much better is it to be a servant to God than to man?

## CHAPTER XXXI.

Vers. **1**. *{And he heard}* His ill usage in Laban's house makes him the more desirous to return into Canaan; so the crosses of this world may make us forecast for a better country, the Canaan above; and to be willing to remove from Mesech and the tents of Kedar, Psal. 120.5. the habitation of ungodly men, to enjoy better company in a better place, Heb. 11.10.

*{words}* The children uttered in words, that which their father dissembled in heart; for the covetous think that whatsoever they cannot snatch to them is pulled from them.

*{hath taken away}* The wicked envying the prosperity of the godly, slander it, as injuriously gotten by themselves, when it was graciously bestowed on them by God. See ver. 8, 9.

*{gotten all this glory}* Worldly men highly esteem of riches as their chiefest glory, Psal. 45.16, 17. though themselves be base in wicked ways of getting, and over-wary keeping of them; but they are only then a glory, when wisdom and righteousness are joined with them, as Prov. 8.18.

V. **2**. *{Countenance}* Though Laban were a subtle and dissembling man, giving good words, Chap. 30.27, 28. without any good intent; yet so great was the grudge of his heart, that the subtlety of his head could no longer conceal it, and so by his countenance, he discovered his ill affection towards Jacob, as well as his sons by their backbiting words: thus by God's goodness are the godly warned to beware of the wicked. See on chap. 45.

*{as before}* Heb. *as yesterday, and the day before.* See annot. on Chap. 30.33.

V. **4**. *{Rachel and Leah}* See on ver. 14.

V. **5**. *{God of my fathers}* That is, the God whom my fathers worshiped, and with whom they were joined by an especial covenant.

V. **6**. *{with all my power}* A faithful and religious servant will be as intentive and laborious in his master's affairs, as in his own; serving him, as Jacob, with all his might, and more than that, he cannot do for himself; and as he could not do more, so could he not endure more for himself, than for his master he did. See ver. 40. This good servants will take for a pattern of pains and patience; to the bad, who are slight and slothful in their master's business, minding their own ease and pleasure, more than their master's profit (though bad masters as Laban was) it may be brought for rebuke.

V. **7**. *{ten times}* It may be taken for many times; as Num. 14.22. not precisely ten, but rather more; for the ewes yeaning twice a year in Mesopotamia, as they do in Italy, Jacob might in the six years' service for his reward in cattle have his wages changed above ten times; but a certain number is put for an uncertain, which is usual in the Scripture; and for this number, see Lev. 26.26. Job 19.3. Zach. 8.23. Neh. 4.12.

*{But God suffered him not}* God's restraint of the wicked, is the protection of the godly. See Gen. 20.6.

V. **8**. *{If he said thus, the speckled shall be}* Before the increase fell to Jacob under divers colors, Chap. 30.32. but Laban thinking that too great a wages for his work, restrained him to lambs of one color; and they likewise multiplying to more than he was willing to allow him, (as if he had thriven by change rather than by regular providence) he changes from that color to another. But though Laban were so changeable that Jacob had just cause to complain of him for it, God is the same in his goodness to him; and so he has the advantage of Laban, what change or choice soever he made, the greatest number fell to Jacob's lot; yea, all that were not separated before, brought forth according to the contract concluded on by covenant betwixt them to be Jacob's.

V. **10**. *{It came to pass}* See on Chap. 30.39.

V. **13**. *{I am the God}* The apparition, ver. 10, 11. and this ver. 13. though reported so near together, were six years asunder in time; for the former was about the beginning of Jacob's last six years' service, this latter at the end of them; and he that is here called God, ver. 11. is called the Angel of God, and this angel was Christ, which appeared to Jacob in Bethel; and hereby appears, that he had taught his wives the fear of God, for he talks as though they knew the thing.

*{of Bethel}* Bethel is the house of God; the God of Bethel, the God of God's house: by which title God approving the name that Jacob gave unto it, Chap. 28.19. and withal accepting of his service and vow which he made in that place, stirs him up to future confidence by former experience of his favor.

*{Vowedst a vow}* God shows himself pleased with his vow; and by mentioning it, stirs him up to a due performance of what he had vowed.

V. **14**. *{Rachel and Leah}* One spoke for both, or both spoke the same thing, as Peter and John, Act. 4.19. but Rachel (though the younger daughter) is named first, as the best beloved, and because she should have been the elder wife by seven years, if either Jacob or she had had their right, Gen. 29.25. so are these two women named, Ruth 4.12. See annot. on ver. 4. and make one of both.

*{yet any portion}* Or, *any more portion*. The daughters of Laban apprehending no profit by their husband's further continuance in his service, or their abode in his house, are willing to forsake him; so is his covetousness requited in its kind; he cares for none but for his profit's sake, and they (though his daughters) care no otherwise for him, than they may reap commodity by continuing with him.

V. **15**. *{As strangers}* Good men entertain strangers courteously, like friends, Gen. 18.3. and 19.2. bad men use their nearest friends, or kindred, as harshly as if they were but strangers.

*{he hath sold us}* For they were given to Jacob in recompense of his service, which is a kind of sale, whereas Laban should have given them a part of his estate in marriage.

*{devoured also our money}* That is, what we might have had in money or money's worth, for the fourteen years' service of our husband, he has spent as his own upon his own occasions.

V. **16**. *{Whatsoever God hath said}* The precedent reasons for removal from Laban's service are human, this is divine, and so better than all the rest; a ready rule to obey God in all cases, which answers all doubts, and may secure us against all afterclaps; while we obey as of duty we may trust him with the success, and so not trouble ourselves with a fearful forecast of offensive consequences to ensue: so these women are ready to do as God ordained, viz. to leave their father, and to go with their husband, Genes. 2.24. hoping to find the comfort in him and their children which was lost in their father, Psal. 45.16.

V. **18**. *{To go to Isaac}* He was long in going, about ten years, by his dwelling at Shechem and Bethel by the way.

V. **19**. *{Rachel had stolen}* Neither out of covetousness, (though haply the images were pretty and precious) nor out of desire to divorce her father from his idols, nor to prevent his divination of their flight by them, but as yet tainted with her native idolatry, it is like she stole them with a superstitious respect unto them. See Chap. 35.2.

*{Images}* Or, *Idols*. For images taken for gods (as these were, ver. 30.) must needs be idols; the word in the original is *Teraphim*, a word of the plural number, because they that addicted themselves to idols, loved them so well, as to have usually more than one of that sort in their houses. Of what figure these images were, it is not certainly known: some take them to be vessels or instruments of brass of the use of dials, whereto was added sometimes the operation of devils, for presage or prediction of future things; but it is more like they were of an human shape, for so it appears, 1 Sam. 19.13. where the same word is used of an image in David's family, where the thing was not abused, as in other places, being kept haply rather for derision than for devotion; with them idolaters consulted concerning secret matters, Ezek. 21.21. from them by the deceits of the devil, or the priests, they received vain and delusive answers, Zech. 10.2. and it is like they expected help and health by them, whence Avenarius derives the Greek word, *Therapeuo*, which signifies both *to worship*, and *to heal*; thus do these images, or *Teraphim*, become perfect idols: and the word is most appropriated to such images, as by the cunning and imposture of the devil were used to give answer to idolatrous people. In Hos. 3. ver. 4. images and *Teraphim* are set down as different things; the word for image is *Matsebah*, which is the same with *Statua*, or *a standing resemblance*, derived from a word signifying *to erect, or set up*, so it may stand for an image in general: but *Teraphim* signifies a peculiar kind of images, as before has been expressed. See on Judg. 17.5.

V. **20**. *{Stole away unawares}* In the original, *Stole away the heart of Laban*, and so the Geneva translation has it; by the heart of Laban, we may conceive either that which Laban set his heart upon, as, his daughters, and Jacob's goods which he had gotten under him, or the gainful service which he had performed to him; or his *Teraphim*, or images which were as gods to him, ver. 30. all these being taken away at once, he might be as Ephraim, without heart, Hos. 7.11. Or, to steal away from Laban his heart, is to steal away without his knowledge, or good will; as ver. 27. Laban says, *Why didst thou flee away secretly, and steal away me*, so it is in the original; the meaning is *from me*; the word *from*, is sometimes expressed, sometimes understood in the Hebrew, making mention of the same thing, as, *Hear thou from heaven*, 1 King. 8.43.

V. **21**. *{Set his face toward}* With a purpose to go that way. See Jer. 50.5. Luke 9.51, 53.

*{Gilead}* The highest hill beyond Jordan, in length stretched out to 50 miles, it begins near the city Jaer, and the rocks of Arnon southward, and runs through two kingdoms, the one of Og, the other of the Amorites; in that dimension of longitude several parts of it have several names, as Gilead, Seir, Hermon and Libanus. Adrichom. places it in the tribe of Manasses, Theatr. terr. sanct. p. 85. See ver. 47.

V. **22**. *{The third day}* Laban's flocks that were kept by his sons, were three days' journey from the cattle committed unto Jacob's custody, Gen. 30.36. So Laban's craft and misconceit of Jacob gave him an advantage for evasion from him; so is the saying of Eliphaz verified, Job 5.12, 13.

V. **23**. *{His brethren}* That is, his kinsmen and countrymen.

*{seven days journey}* To Laban, but by this time to Jacob it was the thirteenth day; for Jacob was gone three days' journey before Laban knew of his departure, and by that time that Laban had gone those three days' journey, Jacob passed on, and made his six days, and then was Laban where Jacob was first set out; from thence pursuing seven days with a swifter pace than Jacob traveled (with his wives, his little ones, and his flocks) he overtook him the seventh day of his own, the thirteenth of Jacob's journey.

V. **24**. *{To Laban in a dream}* The wicked sometimes had apparitions from God, though not for their own, so much as for the godly's sake. See Gen. 20.3, 7. Num. 22.9.

*{good or bad}* In the Hebrew it is *from good to bad*; see chap. 24.50. but the meaning is, *neither good nor bad*; as Gen. 14.23. *from a thred to a shoo latchet*, that is, not so much as either a thread or a shoe latchet. Or by forbidding to speak either good or bad, is meant as if he had said, neither by fair words nor by foul, flattery nor reproaches, promises nor threats, endeavor to bring back Jacob to your house, or to his former condition when he dwelled with you. Thus God watches over the malignity of the wicked, and for the safety of his servants, and makes them bless that would curse, Numb. 23.11. become kind, that came out cruelly minded against them; as Gen. 32.6, 7. and 33.8, 9. See Psal. 39.2.

V. **27**. *{Sent thee away with mirth}* Laban has now changed his place, but not his practice; he plays the hypocrite still, and pretends that as if he had known Jacob's mind, he would have dismissed him with much cheerfulness; whereas if he had foreknown his purpose, he would have put his tarrying irons upon him, without any permission to depart, so long as he could have kept him in the condition of a servant; malice will pick a quarrel where no fault is made, and hypocrisy will pick a thank where no good is meant.

V. **28**. *{Thou hast now done foolishly}* Jacob did very wisely in following of God, and flying from him; and Laban thinks, no doubt, that he was too wise for him, in getting so much substance under him, and getting it from him with his wives and children without his knowledge, and against his mind; so the wicked in their reproaches many times belie their own hearts, to impeach the reputation of the righteous.

V. **29**. *{It is in the power of my hand}* The wicked boasts of his power to do hurt, not considering how the goodness of God is able to make a restraint of his power and spite. See Psal. 52.1. John 19.10, 11.

*{the God of your father}* He was an idolater, and therefore would not acknowledge the God of Jacob's father, or grandfather (who first forsook the idolatry of his father Terah's family) to be his God; and he speaks in the plural number, your father, meaning Jacob and his children, though he call them also his own, ver. 43.

V. **30**. *{Stolen my gods}* It is not probable that Laban having had for twenty years together the society of Jacob, (a man professing the pure worship of the true God, appearing oft-times unto him, and manifesting his favor by so great blessings upon him, that Laban acknowledged God blessed him for his sake, Gen. 30.27.) should be so gross an idolater, as to take these little *Teraphim* or images for gods indeed, who were not able to save themselves from stealing away, being such as the prophet Jeremy derides, Jer. 10.5. yet in that he calls them by the name of gods, it is not unlike that he committed idolatry to them, worshiping the image for God, or God by the image, or the image with God; and seeing that in so long a time of Jacob's abode in his service, he continued so corrupt in his religion, it shows, that idolatry is woefully deeply rooted in the hearts, not only of the silly, but of the subtle worldlings, as Laban was, and therefore is more religiously to be shunned, and more resolutely to be opposed. See on Judg. 17.5.

V. **32**. *{Let him not live}* Hence some collect, that theft, by the law of nature, was to be punished with death; this severe sentence proceeding of innocent confidence, was somewhat too sudden and inconsiderate, whether he means that himself would put the party to death, or give him or her up to the hands of the idolater; if Jacob had restrained that doom to his own deserving, it had been enough to clear him of the theft, but he made it general, and so showed himself more just in his meaning, than wise in his speaking. See Chap. 44.9.

*{before our brethren}* He means some that came with Laban, whom in civility he calls brethren. See Gen. 19.7. and in affiance of his own faithful dealing, makes them judges of Laban's accusation, though as parties with him in that hostile pursuit they were professed enemies to himself. See Act. 4.19.

V. **35**. *{Jacobs tent, and Leahs tent}* The men had tents apart from the women. See annot. on Gen. 24.67. and the women by themselves, according to their distinction, and difference of children and servants: propriety is useful for peace and privacy. See Chap. 23.2. and 24.67.

*{my Lord}* Reverend respects is to be shown to a father, though a bad one, as Laban was, as submission to a master, though he be froward, 1 Pet. 2.18.

*{the custom of women}* She sat upon the idols, and covered them with her coats, pretending for her not rising (to do reverence to her father) the necessity of her present condition according to her sex, Lev. 15.19.

V. **36**. *{Jacob was wroth and chode}* Anger is a passion soon raised, but hardly ruled; the easiest precept in all the Scripture is that of Paul to the Ephesians, Be angry, and the hardest prohibition (that which is joined with it) sin not, Eph. 4.26. for it is never more hard for a man to forbear sin, than when he does not forbear anger; if Jacob kept his displeasure within a warrantable temper (especially so provoked by Laban, who carried himself for the most part liker a cruel master, than a kind uncle or father) his anger is as much to be commended now, as his patience before; and the more, because he does not smother it with silence, as Absalom did his wrath against Amnon, 2 Sam. 13.22. nor sugar it over with sweet words, or shows of good will, as Joab did by Amasa, 2 Sam. 20.9. (which as some conceive is a point of wisdom, but is (as Solomon accounts it) folly, Prov. 10.18.) but chides it out, and so shows himself to be, as he is styled, a plain man, Gen. 25.17. And in this we may take the example of his disposition into our imitation; but then we must take heed that our wrath last not too long, (for though it may be sometimes a guest in the bosom of a wise man, it dwells only in the bosom of fools, Eccles. 7.9.) and that it chide not too loud, with a sharper accent of rebuke than the cause will well bear, and so fall upon foul reproaches, instead of free reproofs.

V. **37**. *{My brethren and thy brethren}* See annot. on ver. 32.

V. **39**. *{I bare the loss}* The careful shepherd should not satisfy for casual losses, yet so unjust was Laban to require it, or Jacob so just as of himself to do it.

V. **41**. *{Thus have I been}* Ver. 38, 39, 40. Jacob shows (Laban's iniquity compelling him to praise himself, and so did Paul, moved thereunto by emulous adversaries, 1 Cor. 15.10. and 2 Cor. 11.1. &c.) what he did and endured in his service, overseeing his flocks for twenty years together; and yet he had but the charge of beasts, how much better are the souls of men, and how then should spiritual pastors rouse up their spirits, and stir up their endeavors, and persist in their vigilant care for the sheep of Christ's flock? How should they watch, and work, and do, and suffer anything, lest any sheep or lamb belonging to Christ's fold should be worried with the wolf? See Heb. 13.17. 1 Pet. 5.2. Isai. 56.10.

*{ten times}* See the annot. on ver. 7.

V. **42**. *{and the fear of Isaac}* In all these titles, the God of my father, the God of Abraham, Jacob's grandfather, and the fear of Isaac, that is, the God of Isaac, he means but one God, but names both his father and grandfather, in regard of the great and especial promises made to them both; and he names his father first as being next unto him, and ascends by him to his grandfather; and being that he could go no higher (for the covenant for the promised land was first made with him) he comes down from him to his father again, and for the God of his father, puts down the fear of Isaac, meaning him whom Isaac feared, Gen. 27.33. for God is the proper object of religious fear. See Isa. 8.13. chap. 41.1. Isai. 8.13. Psal. 135.4.

V. **43**. *{All that thou seest, is mine}* (1 Kin. 20.3.) That is, all the goods and cattle which are within your view, which you look on as your own, are mine; as if Jacob had nothing as his own right, either by desert from him, or gift from God; he makes this brag, that Jacob may think he is beholding to him, if he take not from him the goods he has gotten.

*{what can I do}* He owns his daughters and grandchildren as a tender father and grandfather, and pretends, that being so near of kin to him, they are so dear unto him, that he cannot find in his heart to do them any hurt.

V. **44**. *{Let us make a covenant}* His conscience reproved him of his misbehavior toward Jacob: and therefore moved him to seek peace at his hands.

V. **45**. *{A stone}* So in the original, but the meaning may be stones, (by a figure called Enallage) or a heap of stones. See Gen. 28.11, 18.

*{a pillar}* In testimony of Jacob's true intention to keep the covenant proposed. See Exod. 24.4.

V. **47**. *{Galeed}* So called by anticipation, ver. 25. for until now, upon this occasion, that mountain was not called by that name. It is a long tract of hills extended fifty miles in length, and called at a certain distance by the several names of Gilead, Seir, Hermon and Lebanon; in this place it has two names, the one given in the Syrian tongue by Laban, the other in the Hebrew tongue by Jacob, both having the same signification, viz. *The heap of witness*. See on ver. 21.

V. **48**. *{This heap is a witness}* That is, this heap raised up in remembrance of the covenant betwixt us, will be a memorial or remembrance, which may be alleged by way of witness or testimony to the truth of the covenant concluded betwixt us. In which speech there is a figure called metonymy, whereby the sign is put for the thing signified. See annot. on Chap. 33.20.

V. **49**. *{Mizpah}* A name given of beholding, as men behold out of a watchtower; meaning that God does behold and look both upon the covenant and those that make it, and whether sincerely or no they intend to keep it; Laban gave this name, that he might seem to have some religion, and to bind Jacob, who was religiously minded, to be more observant of his part of the covenant.

V. **50**. *{If thou shalt}* The sense is suspended, and left imperfect, the words of a curse concealed. See annot. on Chap. 14.23. which is usually rather implied than expressed, out of an aversion and unwillingness to mention it, as Chap. 14.23. whence it was, for the word curse, a word of blessing is used, Job 2.9. where according to the original, the words of Job's wife may in the primary interpretation be rendered, *blesse God and dy*, though taken according to her wicked intent, they be translated, *Curse God and dye*: the meaning here may be supplied thus, *If you shall afflict, then God who both knows and rewards wickedness (especially treachery) punish you as you deserve*.

*{take other wives}* (Levit. 18.18.) Having been (while his daughters were with him) a very ill father. See ver. 15. he now pretends a tenderness of affection to them, and conditions with Jacob against that vice, whereunto through covetousness he forced him before.

V. **52**. *{This heap be witness}* See annot. on ver. 48.

V. **53**. *{Of Nahor}* Behold how the idolater mingles the true God with his feigned gods: he says not, the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac but of Abraham, and of Nahor, and their father Terah, for these agreed in the worshiping of false gods, Josh. 24.2. the God in whom Abraham and Isaac agreed, is the true God; but Terah was ancienter than Abraham, and Nahor than Isaac; yet both of them rather idolaters than true believers. Antiquity then (especially if it be but of a few degrees of precedency) is no good proof of the verity of religion; but the child may be of a better religion than his father, or his grandfather.

*{fear of his father Isaac}* See annot. on ver. 42.

V. **54**. *{Eat bread}* Solemn covenants were confirmed by sacrifice; Psal. 50.5. and feasting, Gen. 26.30. the feast though consisting of flesh, is called by the name of bread, because bread is of most use for man's food, and is always one part of the meal, though other meats be never so much varied; bread without them is many times eaten, they without it seldom, or never.

V. **55**. *{Kissed}* An usual manner in many countries to begin their meeting, and conclude their parting with a kiss, as here. See annot. on Chap. 29.11. See also, 2 Sam. 14.33. and Gen. 33.4. Ruth 1.14. 2 Sam. 14.33.

*{blessed them}* There is some seed of knowledge of God in the hearts of the wicked; and an overruling power of Almighty God here appears, in making him, who came forth to pursue Jacob and his company as thieves, to take an affectionate farewell of them with a friendly kiss, and fatherly blessing. See Gen. 33.4. the story of Balaam, Numb. 23.11. and of Paul, Act. 28.4, 5, 6.

## CHAPTER XXXII.

Vers. **1**. *{Angels of God met him}* Not in a dream, but when he was awake they presented themselves unto him in a visible apparition; that these were troops of angels under the president angel of the country of Mesopotamia, and the president angel of the country of Canaan coming with his company to meet each other and his troops, as some affirm, is a presumptuous conceit, and it is like as false as presumptuous.

V. **2**. *{This is Gods host}* He acknowledges God's benefits, who for the preservation of his, sends hosts of angels; and sometimes his assistance is represented with other apparitions, as 2 King. 6.17. The angels are called hosts, that is, companies of soldiers: first, for their number, for they are many, Dan. 7.10. Luk. 2.13. Secondly for their order, for their captain, (Josh. 5.13, 14, 15.) the Lord of hosts who teacheth the hands to war, and the fingers to fight, is most skillful to direct them, and they most observant of his discipline. Thirdly for their power, for one of them in one night was able to slay of the Assyrians' army, an hundred fourscore and five thousand, 2 King. 1.35. Lastly, for their service, which is the defense of God's church, and children, 2 King. 6.17. Psal. 34.7. Dan. 10.20. and the destruction of the wicked, Gen. 19.13. Now though Jacob were secured from the danger of Laban's pursuit, he must not account himself safe without continuance of the divine providence over him; for the godly are always in danger to be assaulted by some enemies, or other, and therefore need a guard of angels, when their estate seems safest; and though one alone, or God himself without their subordinate service could protect them, yet to show his great favor, and to do them more honor, God limits not the charge of them to any one particular angel, but sends an host here to one man, and has made them all ministring spirits to minister unto them, who shall be heirs of salvation, Heb. 1.14. all of them to all, to keep them in their ways, Psal. 91.11. without limitation either of angels, or persons, so that no angel is restrained from a particular ministration to any of the elect; nor any of the elect so allotted to the custody of any angel, that he may not expect the protection of many.

*{Mahanaim}* Two hosts or camps, Cant. 6.13. The word is of the dual number, and the hosts might be two, the one before, the other behind; or the one on the one side, the other on the other side of Jacob and his company; and if we take it in a plural sense, these armies may be thought to compass him about, as Psal. 34.7. howsoever, they placed themselves in such sort as to give Jacob assurance of safety every way, since their service is appointed them by God for the good of the godly, Psal. 91.11.

V. **3**. *{Jacob sent Messengers}* The word Malachim is the same for the angels that came to him, and for the messengers sent by him to his brother: and the word Angel, signifies no more in the literal sense; whence some Jews have grossly mistaken the text, thinking that Jacob sent some of these angels on the errand to Esau; which is a vain conceit, for he directs the messengers what to say, ver. 4. which he would not presume to do unto such angels as God sent unto him, who were angels by nature, that is, heavenly spirits, as well as by name; that is, such as bring messages from one to another; the differences betwixt the one and the other may be observed by the circumstances of the place, and collations of Scriptures.

*{to Esau his brother}* Because he was to pass through his country in his return to Canaan.

*{unto the land of Seir, the Country of Edom}* Here they seem to be the same; but Gen. 36.21. Seir is said to be in the land of Edom, so Seir may be taken for a part of Edom, or Esau's possession which was called Seir, not from Esau, (though he were called Seir for his roughness, as Edom for his redness) for it had that name before Esau's time, Gen. 14.6. but from Seir a Chorite, or Horite, Gen. 36.20.

V. **4**. *{unto my Lord Esau}* (Ver. 18. Chap. 33.8.) He reverenced his brother in worldly things, because he chiefly looked to be preferred in the spiritual promise; and though he had the blessing of the birthright pronounced upon him, yet the time was not yet come that it should be perfectly accomplished; nor did this submissive, either speech or behavior of Jacob to Esau, prejudice his right of primogeniture or birthright, no more than David did his right of royalty, who after he was anointed king, calls Saul, the Lords anointed, and his Master, 1 Sam. 24.6. And in this fair speech of Jacob, he prudently applied himself to the pacification of Esau, ver. 5. see Prov. 15.1. of whom he had cause to fear somewhat of his old grudge and threat, which drove him to take a long journey and hard service for his security from it. See Prov. 25.15.

*{I have sojourned with Laban}* By reporting his condition as banished from his native country so long, he proposes himself as an object rather of pity, than of envy, to his brother.

V. **5**. *{I have oxen}* In mentioning his estate, he brags not of his riches, but shows that he will not be burdensome either to him or his father's house, nor a reproach to their family by his poverty.

V. **6**. *{And the Messengers}* Some upon these words note, that the messengers brought word that Esau was appeased, and that he came to meet him of love and respect; but there is not a word in the text to that purpose, and the fear of Jacob in the next verse shows the contrary.

*{four hundred men with him}* If he came not for mischief, he brought so many for ostentation, or for security; for those that are a terror to many, are afraid of many.

V. **7**. *{Greatly afraid}* Albeit he was comforted by the angels, yet the infirmity of his flesh does appear; the angels appeared unto Jacob betwixt two dangers, when there appeared no need of their protection unto him; now the angels are gone, and his incensed brother comes with four hundred armed men, in all probability to take revenge for a wrong of twenty years' standing. Thus God is pleased to give his servants interchangeable causes of comforts and fears, that they may still be exercised for their spiritual proficiency, and may neither despair in distress nor presume in prosperity.

*{he divided}* The people and the flocks; the greater cattle by themselves, and the lesser by themselves, and some of his company with each sort to drive them together; honest policy (as well as faith and piety) is both lawful and needful in the affairs of God's servants. See Ver. 13, 20. chap. 14.15. and 30.37, 41.

V. **9**. *{O God of my father}* Here, if ever, was a fit time and occasion for Jacob to betake himself to the mediation of the angels, who had lately presented themselves to his view, as military troops, and it was now seasonable to implore their presence to overmatch the forces of his brother; but he knew that was unlawful, and therefore he directs his supplication for safety immediately to the God of his father and grandfather, (without any mention of angels at all;) and he uses their names to quicken and strengthen his faith, by the promises of God unto them, and his covenant with them; for though God sometimes send his servants visible succors in their distress, as 2 King. 6.17. yet that is very rarely, because he would have their hearts ordinarily upheld by faith, and not by sense. See Annot. on chap. 31.41.

V. **10**. *{of the least}* Jacob pleads his merit toward Laban, Chap. 31. from ver. 38. to 41. but having to do with God, he sets a very low esteem of himself, as not deserving the least of God's mercies. See the selfsame dejection of Abraham, Gen. 18.27. and of Mephibosheth, 2 Sam. 9.7, 8. See also Luk. 17.10.

*{all the truth}* That is, not only by teaching him to discern betwixt truth and falsehood; but by showing himself true in his predictions and promises unto him, making them true and right by an answerable event.

*{with my staff}* But poor, like a wayfaring footman that carries all his wealth with him, and yet is not overloaded with his burden.

*{this Jordan}* Which he might see from Mount Gilead, or Galeed, where he last was, Chap. 31.47. and if at that time out of sight, yet not out of mind, and so as present to his memory, he might say, this Jordan.

*{become two bands}* That is, come on, or increased in estate, so that I have two bands, a flock of lesser cattle, and a drove of greater, and two companies of servants to attend and order them. See ver. 7. of this chapter.

V. **11**. *{Deliver me}* Prayer is as a city of refuge to the godly against the malice of the mighty; the readiest means of deliverance out of distress, Psal. 50.15.

*{the mother with the children}* Or, *upon her children*, as Hos. 10.10. meaning he will put all to death; this proverb comes of them who kill the bird together with her young ones, Deut. 22.6.

V. **13**. *{which came to his hand}* (1 Sam. 25.8.) That is, not which his hand fetched in by craft, or guile, or rapine, or wrong, as Hab. 1.15. but which came to his hands, as freely sent or presented him by God's providence, and his blessing upon his labors; or that which was nearest at hand as fit to make a pacifying present.

*{a present}* A liberal present consisting (as some reckon) of five hundred and eighty head of cattle of several kinds; where we may observe the prudence of Jacob in his carriage towards Esau, as well as in his prayer, his faith and piety to God; he prays to God and puts his confidence in him, yet uses human means to serve the divine providence, as well as to preserve himself, and his company: and sending of presents is a good means to that purpose, Prov. 17.8. and Chap. 18.16.

V. **16**. *{every drove by themselves}* Heb. *drove, drove.* See Annot. on Chap. 7.2.

*{a space between}* That Esau's displeasure might be abated by degrees, and so by degrees he might increase in favor, and acceptance with him; a prudent course, and by God's blessing like to take that effect he intended, Chap. 33.8. as indeed it did, Chap. 33.8, 9. See Annot. on Chap. 33.1.

V. **22**. *{eleven sons}* He had a twelfth child, his daughter Dinah, the youngest of all his children, (excepting Joseph) who no doubt was under his provident care with her brethren; but she is not mentioned in this place, either because the female sex is not so much observed in the Scripture, (for they were not entered into the church with a sacrament, as the males were) nor is any of their ages registered or summed up at their death, except Sarah's, (as some have noted) or it may be Dinah was not mentioned, because she was not a mother in Israel, as these eleven sons were fathers.

*{Jabbok}* See Annot. on Deut. 2.37. See also Numb. 21.24. Deut. 3.16. Josh. 12.2. Judg. 11.13.

V. **24**. *{there wrestled a man}* So in appearance; but indeed God, as is implied by Jacob's desire of a blessing from him, ver. 26. and his mention of him by the name of God, vers. 28, 30. who, Hos. 12. is called first God, ver. 3. then an angel, ver. 4. The same angel it was whom Jacob remembers (in his benediction) as his deliverer from all evil, Gen. 48.16. that is, the angel of the covenant, Mal. 3.1. Michael the archangel, Jude 9. that is, Christ; not a created angel, and Jacob's keeper, as some conceive.

*{wrestled}* Not only with spiritual strugglings, tears, and prayers, Hos. 12.4. but with corporal also, wherein God assailed him with one hand, and upheld him by the other.

*{until the break of day}* This wrestling was by night, (but at what time of the night it does not appear) and took up about break of day, for it was intended for a private conflict without spectators; none must be witnesses of it but Jacob, nor must Jacob fully know with whom he wrestles, and therefore he departed before clear light appeared to discover him to the servants of Jacob, or any other that should come that way.

V. **25**. *{when he saw}* This is spoken after the manner of men, whose knowledge comes to them by time, and experience, whereas God by his pure and perfect act of intelligence knows all things, not by degrees, or successively, but perfectly and at once.

*{that he prevailed not}* Not because he could not, but because he would not, as Gen. 19.22. for in comparison of him Jacob was but a worm, as he is called, Isa. 41.14. easily trodden on, and crushed under his foot; and God gave him strength to resist, and hold out, so that whosoever gave over first, the victory was his who gave the vigor to prevail; and if the words had been, he could not prevail, they must have been understood, not for any overmatching of his power, but for the resolution of his will, which, in regard of his decree to order the conflict thus, must needs be so. See Mar. 6.5.

*{out of joint}* By the strength that was given to Jacob to wrestle, and to prevail with God, he might take encouragement to meet with his brother Esau now marching towards him, that the news of his approach might not too much perplex him; and that he might not be too much puffed up with the glory, and success of such a single combat, he is made sensible of his own human frailty, and of his power who strove with him, by a maim in his thigh; so Paul lifted up with revelations to the third heaven, lest he should be exalted above measure, 2 Cor. 12.7. felt a thorn in the flesh, and the buffetings of Satan.

V. **26**. *{Let me go}* See Annot. on Exod. 32.10. See also Deut. 9.14. and Luk. 24.28, 29.

*{for the day breaketh}* See Annot. on ver. 24.

*{I will not let thee go}* Though by this hurt in his thigh he was made more weak, yet was he strong, 2 Cor. 12.10. so strong, as to wrestle again for a blessing; and this was a most vehement wrestling with weeping, and supplication, as Hosea notes, Chap. 12.4. The power of prayer is next to Almighty, and by this sometimes are the hands of the Almighty, as it were, bound to the peace, when he has a quarrel with his people, Exo. 32.10. Deut. 9.14.

*{except thou bless me}* This example is many ways appliable to the state of the Christian church; there is a night of wrestling and afflictions, and a day of blessing; there is a mixture of strength, and infirmity in the best; there is an holy striving with God by importunity of prayer, Rom. 15.30. and an holy violence to be used for the kingdom of heaven, Mat. 11.12. and in striving for that, we strive for a blessing; for with a blessing we shall be admitted to it, Mat. 25.34. and with blessings abundantly furnished in it.

V. **27**. *{What is thy name?}* The angel being God, asks not this question, as man, out of ignorance, for he knew it well enough, as he did what was become of Abel, when he asks of his brother Cain where he was, Gen. 4.9. but he asked of his name, to take an occasion for what himself meant to say of the change of his name.

V. **28**. *{no more Jacob, but Israel}* (Chap. 35.10.) That is, *no more only Jacob*, (for that word must be understood, as Jer. 7.22, 23.) for he was often called Jacob, after this; or, *rather Israel than Jacob*, as Hos. 6.6. Exod. 16.2, 8. For after this he was chiefly called Israel, and his posterity more usually the children of Israel, than the children of Jacob and familiarly Israelites, not Jacobites. Or this may be a precept as well as a prophecy; and though all divine prophecies be fulfilled as they are meant, yet all precepts are not performed as they are enjoined. The name Israel, imports (as the angel expounds it) *a princely power with God*; the change of names in the godly is an argument of favor with God, and of honor with men, and an incitement to change from bad to good, from good to better. See Gen. 17.5, 15. The name Israel, comes of *Sarah*, *he has prevailed*, and *El*, *God*, according to the reason rendered in the text. See on Ch. 46.2.

*{and with men}* Having power with God, you shall prevail with men, as with Laban before, so now with Esau your brother, though he may seem to overmatch you, both in the number and power of your people.

V. **29**. *{Tell me, I pray thee, thy name}* God appeared to Jacob at least twice before this, yet before now he did not ask him his name. The reason whereof may be, that Jacob might take occasion to return upon him with the same question, not doubting but he would give himself some peculiar name, whereby he might the better both remember and honor him. See Judg. 13.17.

*{wherefore is it that thou dost ask after my Name}* The angel will succor his necessity, and strengthen him against adversity, but not serve his curiosity; it was not more curiously done in him that asked after the name of this angel, than in many who take upon them to tell the causes why the angel did conceal it. That some angels had names, it is plain by Luk. 1.19, 26. and that the angel of the covenant, Christ Jesus, had also a name before his incarnation, appears, Dan. 10.21. where he is named Michael, and that name is repeated, Jude ver. 9. Rev. 12.7. but whether all the angels have particular names (which may be so if God please, for he may call both angels and stars by their names, Psal. 147.4. in a literal sense) and why the angel in this place would not tell his name is uncertain; it may be the name here meant, was that which was not to be revealed till afterward. See Exod. 6.3. Or that Jacob must be taught humility, (and we by his example) in setting modest bounds to his inquiries, and contenting himself with ignorance of that which God will have hid. See Judg. 13.18. 1 Sam. 6.19. Rom. 12.3.

V. **30**. *{Called the name of the place, Peniel}* That is, the face of God, not that God's essence is discernible by any, but this vision in human form, in comparison of other apparitions, was more plain and familiar, with face to face, as those that wrestle, or as when a man talks with his friend in presence. See Exod. 33.11.

*{face to face}* See Annot. on Exod. 33.11.

*{and my life is preserved}* It has been a conceit of great antiquity (it may be from this place) that men could not see God but with peril of life, so thought Manoah, Judg. 13.22. Yet there is no instance of any one dying upon such a sight; but Exod. 33.20. the Lord himself says, There shall no man see me and live; by which may be meant, that the vision of God is not in this life, but in the other; so that unless a man die, he shall not live to see such a sight, for God is indeed invisible to carnal eyes, 1 Tim. 6.16. See chap. 16.13. Psal. 17.15. 1 Cor. 13.12.

V. **31**. *{He halted}* The faithful so overcome their temptations, that they feel the smart thereof, to the intent that they should not glory, but in their humility. See on ver. 26. And this shows, that he prevailed not with the angel by his own ability. Some think he was cured of his maim before he met his brother; yet is not any person to be despised for any such defect; though the typical priesthood admitted of none to minister at the altar, that had any bodily blemish, Levit. 21.18, 21. yet is none less acceptable with God for it; and though Jacob delighted more in the outside of Rachel than of Leah, because she was more beautiful, if she had not a better inside also, God esteemed them both alike: neither the blindness of Isaac, nor the lameness of Mephibosheth, nor the leprosy of Naaman (and we may take in any other, either defect or deformity, that was not willfully contracted by men's own wickedness, as the redness of eyes in a drunkard, Prov. 23.29.) made them less beloved of God. The use of such infirmities, is (to those that have them not) matter of thanksgiving to Almighty God, who makes the difference; and to those that have them, to be humbled by them, and withal, to endeavor a recompense of their bodily blemishes, with an advantage of spiritual graces and endowments of their minds.

V. **32**. *{unto this day}* The remembrance of this story was kept by a general abstinence of the Israelites from eating of that part of the thigh (in any of the creatures) which in Jacob was sinew-shrunk; and this continued until Moses wrote this story without any intimation of fault or folly therein; and to this day the Jews observe it, though with much vanity and superstition, as they do other observances, whether of history or religion: and indeed the story of God's wrestling, is most memorable, wherein, though profane wit may find somewhat to cavil at, as if such a conflict with man were too mean a business for Almighty God, yet religious wisdom will consider, that Gods thoughts are not mans thoughts, nor his wayes mans wayes, Isai. 55.8. For he chooseth the foolish things of the world (as the world judges them) to confound the wise, and the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty, 1 Cor. 1.27. If human wit had been to set down a sacrament for the patriarchs, it would have despised such a one as circumcision; but God chooses also the base things of the world, and things which are despised, and things which are not, to bring to nought the things that are, ver. 28. And for this descending of the Son of God to this wrestling with Jacob, what is it to that humiliation of his in being born in a stable, to his stooping down to wash his own servants' feet, Joh. 13.5. to his making himself of no reputation, and humbling himself to obedience, even unto death, the death of the cross? Phil. 2.7, 8.

## CHAPTER XXXIII.

Vers. **1**. *{Divided}* That if the one part were assailed, the other might escape. See Annot. on Chap. 32.19. This he does, making human prudence subservient and subordinate to divine providence.

V. **2**. *{Foremost}* He ranks them according to their right, and his own respect unto them; they are set before in a time of danger, who in time of safety come behind.

V. **3**. *{Before them}* He followed the first company which consisted of the handmaids and their children, and went before the other company where were his wives and their children: or, there were three troops of presents to Esau, and these because sent at the same time, and being near together, might go for the first troop. See Chap. 32. from ver. 16. to the 20. inclusively; and if all these made the first troop, his wives and concubines with their children, might make the second, and to them he was the leader; wherein he shows himself as a good pastor, more chary of his charge than of himself, putting himself nearest to the peril, and keeping them as far off as he could. See Joh. 10.11.

*{bowed himself}* By this gesture he partly did reverence to his brother, and partly prayed to God to mitigate his wrath; for the heart may be exercised in devotion to God, while the body performs an outward ministry to man. See Neh. 2.4. Of Jacob's homage to Esau, see Annot. on Chap. 32.4.

*{seven times}* That is, many times, a certain number for an uncertain; of ten times see Chap. 31.7. and the Annot. upon it.

V. **4**. *{Esau ran &c.}* Here be many expressions of reconciliation; too many, too emphatical and forcible to be thought feigned in a man that had neither occasion nor disposition to dissemble; and herein Jacob's advised prudence, and soft language, and submissive behavior served under God's providence to bring this to pass, that he might prevail with men, as well as with God, according to the note set upon his name, Gen. 32.28. Thus when a man's ways please the Lord, the ungodly that are his enemies may be made his friends, Prov. 16.7.

V. **9**. *{I have enough}* Though Esau were a bad man, in this respect there are many worse, who have never enough, Eccles. 4.8. Prov. 30.15.

V. **10**. *{If I have found, &c.}* If indeed you are fully reconciled unto me, receive this present from me.

*{present}* The Hebrew word is *Minchah*, signifying properly, *a gift*, which is given to God or to man, as a superior, with profession of the excellency of him to whom it is given, and the subjection of him that gives it.
