Thirdly, some conceive they avoid the inconveniences last mentioned, by saying, that Abraham is not here to be taken in the nominative case, but in the genitive, understanding Jacob the grandchild of Abraham; for the word son, or grandchild, may as well be understood, as the word brother, 2 Sam. 21:19, where Elhanan is said to slay Goliath the Gittite, that is, *the brother of Goliath*, as the word is supplied, 1 Chron. 20:5, or as the word sister, 2 Sam. 21:8, where it is said, *he took the five sons of Michal*, that is, *the sister of Michal*, for she had no children, 2 Sam. 6:23, or as the word mother, Mark 15:40, as is noted afterwards; all which words, mother, brother and sister, are omitted by a figure called ellipsis, or eclipse, which is clearer in the Greek by the article of the genitive case, than in the Hebrew which has no such distinction by various terminations of cases, as the Greek tongue has. Others say, the name Abraham may be taken in the nominative case. And indeed the name of the parents or progenitors, is sometimes put for the posterity, as the name of Israel or Jacob is put for his offspring, many degrees of descent distant from him: and the name of David is put for the Messiah the descendant of David, Jer. 30:9, Ezek. 34:23. And Joseph is put for his two sons Ephraim and Manasseh, Gen. 48:15, and so David is named where Rehoboam is meant, 1 Kings 12:16, and Abijah the son of Rehoboam, is called Rehoboam, in the report of the war betwixt Jeroboam and him, when Rehoboam was dead, as will appear by comparing 2 Chron. 13:3, with 1 Kings 15:6. Now by such an exposition, though Stephen’s speech (if that were his meaning) might be freed from error, yet if he were not understood in such a sense (which is not obvious to an ordinary apprehension, and hardly light upon without study) he might by the hearers be thought to falsify, in putting one name for another; therefore some endeavor to remove the doubt by that which follows.

In the third doubt, which is concerning Hamor: where were three scruples: First, whether he were father or son to Shechem. According to the Vulgar Latin, and the Geneva, it is *the son of Shechem*; others say, *the father of Shechem*; the original says neither, but *tou Sychem*, that is, *of Sechem*, which in respect of grammar, may be either; but the original story, Josh. 24:32, (whence the word must be supplied) says, *the father of Shechem*: the like construction we have, Matt. 1:16, and 10:2–3, and Luke 24:10, where we read *Mary of James*, which is made up by addition of a word, *Mary the mother of James*, Mark 15:40. The second, whether the father of Ephron were called Hamor, so some say, that Zohar Ephron’s father, with whom Abraham bargained for the field of Machpelah, chap. 23:17, was called Hamor; and so they think the difficulty of this place is best cleared, making the burial place to be that of Abraham’s, not that of Jacob’s purchase: But this is yet too short to reach home to the removal of the doubt; for though it be true, that it is not strange in Scripture for one man to have divers names, yet it does not appear to be so in this case, nor that this Hamor had a son called Shechem, as that Hamor, of whom Jacob bought his portion of ground, had; where we are to answer to the third scruple, which is, Why Shechem only of Hamor’s sons is mentioned, when others, and not he, made the sale of the ground which Jacob bought? Answer. Shechem was amongst Hamor’s sons of chief note and account; for it is said, *he was more honourable then all the house of his fathers*, Gen. 34:19, and since he is named, the rest not mentioned, and it is most probable that he had most to do in this business, and that the rest consented to his transaction.

The sum of all is, That whatsoever contradiction may seem to be betwixt the report of Stephen, and the story of the Old Testament, Luke relating only what Stephen said, is a true historian, though Stephen were not. Secondly, that by the second answer to the second doubt, a sudden slip of memory in Stephen may be confessed without inconvenience, or avoided by the third answer. And if (as some say) the father of Ephron had two names, and Hamor was one of them (which some learned men think the readiest way to resolve the doubt) that may sway the resolution for Abraham’s purchase, as the third answer to the second doubt does for Jacob’s.
